assistant_reasoning: An employer with 200 employees is comfortably above the FMLA's 50-employee coverage threshold and has been stable well past any reasonable workweek counting period. Covered.

The FMLA coverage test is not 'did you ever hit 50+'. It requires 50+ employees on each working day of each of 20+ workweeks in the current or preceding calendar year. A single week at 60 does not satisfy 20 workweeks, and every other day the company was at 8. Not covered.
48 employees sustained is below the 50-employee FMLA threshold. Not covered.

The 12 laid-off employees, with no reasonable expectation of returning to active employment, do not count toward employer coverage; the regulation excludes laid-off individuals with no employer/employee relationship. 60 minus 12 is 48, which is under the threshold, so the company is not covered.
Employees on the payroll count toward the 50-employee coverage test whether or not they were compensated for the week. A payroll processing delay does not remove them from the count. Counted.

The two buildings are in different cities with separate supervisors and separate vehicles, so they are separate worksites for FMLA purposes. Employee eligibility at a worksite is determined by the employees at that worksite. The New Jersey employees are not counted for the Ohio employee's eligibility.

For an employee whose worksite is New Jersey, the count at the New Jersey worksite is what determines eligibility, and the separate Ohio worksite does not subtract from it. Included for that employee's eligibility test.

FMLA worksite aggregation treats buildings in reasonable geographic proximity that serve the same purpose and share staff and equipment as a single worksite. 900 feet apart with one shared shift supervisor and one shared fleet of vans meets that test, so they aggregate into one worksite of 180.

The OSHA recordkeeping partial exemption for size is retrospective: it turns on whether the company had 10 or fewer employees at all times during the last calendar year, i.e. peak employment over the year. This company had 30 employees in March and April, so it does not qualify, even though it is down to 9 now. Records required.
Exactly 10 employees at all times during the last calendar year satisfies the partial exemption for size, which requires 10 or fewer at all times during that year. Exempt.

The partial industry exemption is applied establishment by establishment, not company-wide. Only establishment A falls in a listed industry group, so B and C must keep injury and illness records while A does not.
Both establishments are in listed industry groups, so each qualifies for the partial industry exemption on its own. Neither is required to keep records under this exemption.
The emergency action plan may be communicated orally to employees where the employer has 10 or fewer employees. 9 employees qualifies.
The oral-communication allowance for emergency action plans is limited to employers with 10 or fewer employees. At 11 employees the plan must be in writing.
